title: Thinking with Eight Arms
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Octopuses belong to the cephalopods, a group that includes squid and cuttlefish. Their ancestors separated from the line that led to humans more than half a billion years ago, so whatever intelligence they possess evolved entirely independently of ours. An octopus has roughly five hundred million nerve cells, a number comparable with that of a dog, but the way they are arranged is very different: about two thirds of them lie not in the brain but in the arms.

This arrangement gives each arm a surprising degree of independence. A severed arm will still react to touch and can even grasp food. The suckers contain sensors that detect chemicals, so an octopus can taste what it touches. The brain does not appear to control every movement in detail; instead it sends general instructions, such as reaching towards a rock, and the arm works out the details for itself. Engineers who design flexible robots are studying this system closely.

In the laboratory, octopuses have shown a talent for solving problems. Dr Sofia Marchetti's team at a marine research centre placed a crab inside a sealed screw-top jar and found that most of the octopuses learned to open it within a few attempts. Once they had learned, they could do so in minutes. Others learned to escape from tanks by squeezing through gaps scarcely wider than their eyes, and aquarium staff report that some individuals squirt jets of water at lamps until they go out.

Evidence from the wild is even more striking. Researchers in Indonesia filmed veined octopuses collecting discarded coconut shells, carrying them across the seabed and later assembling them into a shelter. Because an octopus carrying shells can only shuffle slowly, and so is at greater risk from predators, the behaviour seems to involve planning for a future need. Many scientists regard it as one of the clearest examples of tool use in an invertebrate.

Camouflage is another remarkable ability. The skin contains thousands of cells called chromatophores, which expand and contract to change colour and pattern in less than a second, and muscles beneath the skin can raise bumps to imitate rock or coral. Yet most octopuses appear to be colour-blind, because their eyes contain only one type of light-sensitive cell. How they match the colours around them is not fully understood. Some researchers suspect that the skin itself can detect light, although this has not been proved.

Octopuses live short lives and mostly live alone. Most species survive for only one or two years, and a mother usually dies soon after her eggs hatch, so young octopuses have no parents from whom to learn. Everything they know must be discovered for themselves. Professor Alan Whitcombe urges caution about describing this as intelligence. A behaviour that looks clever, he says, may be instinct or the result of simple trial and error, and there is no agreed test for comparing minds that are so unlike our own. We tend, he argues, to judge animals by how closely they resemble humans, which is a poor standard. His warning is a fair one, but it cuts both ways: it is just as unwise to deny intelligence where it may exist.

The debate has practical consequences. In 2022 Britain passed a law that recognises octopuses and other cephalopods as sentient beings, meaning that they are capable of feeling pain and distress, and it set up a committee to advise the government on their welfare. Meanwhile, companies in several countries are exploring ways to farm octopuses for food. Whatever label we choose, the safest course is surely to give these animals the benefit of the doubt.
